newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: More "stolen" Aborigines sue Australian government.
newsitem.headline: More "stolen" Aborigines sue Australian government.

text.p: Aborigines "stolen" from their parents by past Australian governments stepped up legal claims for compensation on Tuesday, angry at Canberra's recent refusal to even apologise for the practice, a lawyer said.
The lawyer, acting for hundreds of Australia's so-called "stolen generations", said he had filed 96 more writs against the government in the High Court in the Northern Territory on Tuesday.
The fresh writs come on top of 563 writs filed late last year in the Northern Territory, said Matthew Storey, of the publicly funded Aboriginal Legal Aid Service in Darwin.
Similar writs have been filed across the country.
Each writ seeks the government to accept liability for the past policy of forcibly taking Aboriginal children from their families and assimilating them into the white community.
The practice continued into the 1960s and was condemned last week as attempted genocide by Australia's human rights authority.

"The human rights report was very significant to the 'stolen generations' community because finally it was official recognition of what happened to them," Storey told Reuters by telephone from Darwin, the Northern Territory capital.
Prime Minister John Howard has rejected the report's recommendation that the government make a formal apology and compensate the tens of thousands of victims of assimilation.
Howard instead offered a personal apology last week, saying he felt deep sorrow for the past injustices.
But Storey said his clients, ranging in age from a woman in her 90s to a woman in her 30s, felt Howard had broken his pledge to thoroughly examine the report before making any decisions.
"The filing of these additional actions is appropriate because clearly the Commonwealth government has rejected the major findings of the Human Rights Commission report out of hand," he said.
In the Northern Territory, another wave of writs could yet be filed. "There may be some hundreds more...in the end," Storey said.
The first hearing into one of the Northern Territory cases could begin early next year, he added.
Around Australia, the national government as well as state governments have either been sued or threatened with legal action by "stolen generation" Aborigines.
Concerns over the issue of compensation were raised with Howard on Tuesday at a meeting of government legislators in Canberra, but the meeting endorsed his handling of the issue.
